To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the majority of the ORFs identified in S. cerevisae genome sequencing projects encode nonessential proteins; (2) the deletion of a single ORF is sufficient to cause a growth defect in 40 percent of cases; and (3) the deletion of an ORF is sufficient, in some cases, to cause a specific phenotype, such as a defect in mating, meiosis or sporulation

1) 17 percent of the yeast genome encodes essential genes, 2) more than half of the yeast genome is non-essential and 3) the phenotypes of more that 50 percent of the non-essential genes can be predicted from the sequence of their protein products.
1) the deletion of one of the 2026 non-essential ORFs in the S. cerevesiae genome is not lethal for 83 percent of the ORFs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the systematic analysis of the yeast genome by the use of a collection of deletion strains, which is a new approach to the functional analysis of the yeast proteome.
the functional analysis of the yeast genome.
the development of new methods for the functional analysis of the yeast genome, and the use of these methods to determine the functions of many yeast genes.

the deletion of a gene is essential for growth in rich medium if the deletion strain does not grow at all in rich medium.
the majority of the ORFs are non-essential for growth in rich media.
the vast majority of the ORFs are not essential for viability in either rich or simple medium and that a substantial proportion of them are not essential for growth.

40 percent of the S. Cerevisiae genome is required for normal growth.
the deletion of a single gene in yeast often results in a growth defect.
40 percent of the ORFs are essential for growth in rich media and that 40 percent show growth defects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now use the deletion data set to predict functions for many of the remaining ORFs.
a large proportion of the yeast genome encodes genes whose products are not essential for growth on rich medium but are important for growth on minimal medium.
we can now begin to understand how the functions of these genes relate to each other and to the functions of known genes.
